dedupe_keys.name: strengthening post hurricane supply chain resilience observations from hurricanes harvey irma and maria 2017

description: This National Academies consensus study examines how supply chains for essential goods held up, or failed, after Hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria in 2017. It covers food and groceries, fresh water, fuel, electricity and pharmaceutical and medical goods, describing how each system was affected, where effects were common or different between places, and which interdependencies, nodes or sub-systems amplified or limited disruption. The producer is the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, through an ad hoc committee chaired by James G. Featherstone. Coverage is Houston and Galveston in Texas, Miami and Fort Lauderdale in Florida, Puerto Rico, and St. Thomas and St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The 2020 report is free to download as a PDF from the National Academies Press or to read online, under the Press's copyright. Caveats: the study is qualitative and based on observations and stakeholder input, not shipment data, and conditions in Puerto Rico after Maria were exceptional in scale and duration. Simulation uses: defining disruption scenarios and interdependencies for food, fuel and medical supply network models, and testing how distribution depends on power, ports and roads after a hurricane. Related records: the Hurricane Ida food distribution study (case_study-hurricane-ida-new-orleans-food-distribution) shows food aid at city scale, and PyTradeShifts (model-pytradeshifts) models trade networks.
